about: Building materials (roadmap BT3a): Stone (forms, techniques and the great building stones of the isles) and Mortar and render (lime mortar, harling, roughcast, stucco). Fields as bidb/building_materials.py.

period.text: Mortared rubble walling came with the Romans, who used rubble masonry widely: 43 is the year of the Roman conquest (Roman Britain lasted 43-410), not a dated wall. Unmortared rubble walls are much older (see dry-stone walling). Still used.

examples.name: Holy Trinity Church, Colchester (tower)
examples.note: pre-Conquest 11th-century tower built of Roman rubble

sources.title: Rubble (FISH Building Materials, concept 98165)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Rough, unhewn, undressed building stones with irregular faces, generally not laid in regular courses.

sources.title: Rubble masonry
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Romans made extensive use of rubble masonry, calling it opus caementicium

sources.title: Roman Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The occupation lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD.

sources.title: Anglo-Saxon architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The tower of Holy Trinity Church in Colchester, Essex has a pre-Conquest 11th-century tower built out of Roman rubble

period.text: Squared, dressed stone came with the Romans: 43 is the year of the Roman conquest, not a dated wall. Escomb church (built between 650 and 800) reused the squared masonry of a Roman fort, and Bede says such churches were built 'in the manner of the Romans'. Still used.

examples.name: Escomb Church
examples.note: built between 650 and 800 of large roughly-dressed squared stones, much of it from the Roman fort at Binchester

sources.title: Ashlar (FISH Building Materials, concept 97722)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A square, hewn or worked, high class freestone which can be 'freely' cut and is laid in horizontal courses with vertical joints.

sources.title: Ashlar
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is cut and dressed stone worked to achieve a specific form, typically rectangular

sources.title: Roman Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The occupation lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD.

sources.title: Escomb Church
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Much of the squared masonry was taken from the nearby Roman fort at Vinovia (Binchester).

sources.title: Escomb Church
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: are consistent with it having been built between AD 650 and 800

sources.title: Anglo-Saxon architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: was undertaken morem Romanorum, "in the manner of the Romans", in explicit contrast to existing traditions of timber construction

materials.name: Dry-stone walling

period.text: The stone-walled field system of the Céide Fields, County Mayo, carbon-dated to 3800 BC, is the earliest dry-stone work a source names in the isles; the dry-stone village of Skara Brae (occupied from about 3180 BC) is near contemporary. Wallers are still in demand.

regions.text: Upland Britain and Ireland where stone lies in the soil or outcrops, above all the west of Ireland (Connemara, the Burren); field walls are called dykes in Scotland

materials.technology: Built of stones cleared from the fields, needing no lime; wire fencing later made new walls far cheaper to do without.

examples.name: Céide Fields
examples.note: field system of dry stone walls under the peat, County Mayo

examples.name: Skara Brae
examples.note: Neolithic village built in dry stone

examples.name: Mourne Wall
examples.note: 22-mile wall in the Mourne Mountains, County Down

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is a method of building structures from stones without any mortar to bind them together

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In County Mayo, Ireland, an entire field system made from dry stone walls, since covered in peat, has been carbon-dated to 3800 BC.

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These are near contemporary with the dry stone constructed Neolithic village of Skara Brae and the chambered cairns of Scotland.

sources.title: Skara Brae
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: occupation of Skara Brae began about 3180 BC

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Dry stone walls are characteristic of upland areas of Britain and Ireland where rock forms natural outcrops or large stones exist in quantity in the soil.

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: When used as field boundaries, dry stone structures are more commonly known as dykes in Scotland

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They are especially abundant in the West of Ireland, particularly Connemara.

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many older walls were constructed from stones and boulders cleared from fields during preparation for agriculture (field stones)

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Fields can be fenced with much less time and expense using modern wire fencing compared to stone walls

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As a result of the increasing appreciation of the landscape and heritage value of dry stone walls, wallers remain in demand, as do the walls themselves.

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Notable examples include the Mourne Wall, a 22-mile (35 km) wall in the Mourne Mountains in County Down, Northern Ireland

sources.title: Dry stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Traditional turf-roofed Hebridean blackhouses were constructed using the double-wall dry stone method.

materials.name: Flint and knapped flint

period.text: The Late Roman fort at Burgh Castle, Norfolk, built of flint in lime mortar and dated to the third century (250 stands for that century), is the earliest flint building a source names. Decorative knapped flint flourished in the 15th and early 16th centuries; flint is still used.

regions.text: Southern England without good building stone, above all East Anglia, and the chalk country through Hampshire, Sussex, Surrey and Kent to Somerset

materials.technology: Used where there was no good local building stone and brick-making came late; knapping flints flush and square is skilled work with much waste, so knapped flint marks high-status buildings.

examples.name: Burgh Castle Roman fort
examples.note: Late Roman Saxon Shore fort, third century

sources.title: Flint (FISH Building Materials, concept 97921)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Hard, durable, dark grey stone, the purest native form of silica, which can either be used decoratively or as a main material. Predominantly found in East Anglia and the South East.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Flint, knapped or unknapped, has been used from antiquity (for example at the Late Roman fort of Burgh Castle in Norfolk) up to the present day as a material for building stone walls, using lime mortar

sources.title: Burgh Castle
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The fort, which is a possible site for Gariannonum, dates to the third century and was part of the Saxon Shore fortifications

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was most common in the parts of southern England where no good building stone was available locally, and where brick-making was not widespread until the late Middle Ages.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is especially associated with East Anglia, but also used in chalky areas stretching through Hampshire, Sussex, Surrey and Kent to Somerset.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many different decorative effects have been achieved by using different types of knapping or arrangement and combinations with stone (flushwork), especially in the 15th and early 16th centuries.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Because knapping flints to a relatively flush surface and size is a highly skilled process with a high level of wastage, flint finishes typically indicate high status buildings.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Flint was used in the construction of many churches, houses, and other buildings, for example, the large stronghold of Framlingham Castle.

materials.name: Flushwork

period.text: Flushwork begins in the early 14th century: St Ethelbert's Gate, Norwich, begun in 1316-17, is the earliest important surviving example a source names. Its peak was the wool boom of about 1450 to the 1520s; revived in the 19th century and still sometimes used.

regions.text: Parts of southern England and especially East Anglia (Norfolk, Suffolk); chequerwork also in Wiltshire

materials.technology: Costly in labour but cheaper than importing enough stone to build or face a whole building; the pale stone was often limestone shipped from Caen.

examples.name: St Ethelbert's Gate, Norwich
examples.note: begun 1316-17, flushwork on all four elevations

examples.name: Holy Trinity Church, Long Melford
examples.note: flushwork over most of the body of the church

sources.title: Flushwork (FISH Components, concept 137784)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: The use of knapped flint applied to a wall to form a decorative pattern.

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is characteristic of the external walls of medieval buildings – most of the survivors being churches – in parts of Southern England and especially East Anglia.

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Flushwork begins in the early 14th century, but the peak period was during the wool boom between about 1450 and the English Reformation of the 1520s

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The technique continued in occasional use, and saw a major revival in the 19th century, and is still sometimes used in a modern style today

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Although the labour cost of creating flushwork was high, it was still cheaper than importing the large quantity of stone necessary to build or face the entire structure.

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The stone usually used is a light limestone, often imported by sea and river from Caen in Normandy or other continental sources

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This style is a characteristic of Wiltshire architecture, both vernacular and ecclesiastical.

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: St Ethelbert's Gate at Norwich Cathedral is one of the most important surviving examples of early flushwork, begun in 1316–17 and completed the following decade.

sources.title: Flushwork
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Few churches have flushwork all over the main body of the building. An exception is Holy Trinity Church, Long Melford.

materials.name: Galleting

period.text: Eton College (about 1441) is the earliest dated galleting a source names; parts of Windsor Castle (undated) and the Tower of London (about 1514) were also galleted. Some writers put its heyday in the 17th and 18th centuries; it declined through the 19th century (1900 stands for the end of that decline, not a dated last use).

regions.text: South East England between the North and South Downs (sandstone) and Norfolk (flint)

examples.name: Tower of London
examples.note: galleted about 1514

materials.note: Sources disagree on when it was most used (late medieval, or the 17th and 18th centuries) and on why: wedges for thick mortar joints, decoration, or superstition. Historic Scotland's advice note treats the pinning stones as structural.

sources.title: Galleting
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is an architectural technique in which spalls (small pieces of stone) are pushed into wet mortar joints during the construction of a masonry building

sources.title: Galleting
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, galleting can be found almost exclusively in the South East between the North and South Downs, where sandstone is common, and in the county of Norfolk, where flint is common.

sources.title: Galleting
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Historical records indicate that parts of Windsor Castle (n.d.), Eton College (c. 1441), and the Tower of London (c. 1514) were galleted with flint or oyster shells.

sources.title: Galleting
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some sources associate the technique with late medieval building construction, while others suggest that galleting was used mostly in the 17th and 18th centuries before declining in popularity over the course of the 19th century.

materials.name: Bath stone

period.text: Used in the Roman period (43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for 'Roman') and the Middle Ages; Ralph Allen promoted it in Bath in the early 18th century and it built the Georgian city. Some quarries are still worked.

regions.text: Quarried and mined around Bath (Combe Down, Bathampton Down) and in Wiltshire (Box, Corsham); used throughout southern England

materials.technology: A freestone that can be sawn in any direction; mined by room and pillar, and Allen's railway and wharf on the Kennet and Avon Canal carried it to London.

examples.name: Prior Park
examples.note: Ralph Allen's mansion, built to show off the stone

sources.title: Bath stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 97737)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Even grained, poorly fossiliferous, light brown/cream coloured, oolitic limestone. Quarried in the Bath area.

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: originally obtained from the Middle Jurassic aged Great Oolite Group of the Combe Down and Bathampton Down Mines under Combe Down, Somerset, England

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Bath stone has been used extensively as a building material throughout southern England, for churches, houses, and public buildings such as railway stations.

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the Roman and medieval periods, Bath stone was extensively used on domestic and ecclesiastical buildings, as well as civil engineering projects such as bridges.

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some quarries are still in use, but the majority have been converted to other purposes or are being filled in.

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An important feature of Bath stone is that it is a freestone, one that can be sawn or 'squared up' in any direction

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the early 18th century, Ralph Allen promoted the use of the stone in Bath itself, and demonstrated its potential by using it for his own mansion at Prior Park.

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Allen built a railway line from his mine on Combe Down which carried the stone down the hill

sources.title: Bath stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lancaster House was built from Bath stone in 1825

materials.name: Portland stone

period.text: Quarried on Portland since Roman times (43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for 'Roman'); shipped to London in the 14th century; an industry from the early 17th century (the Banqueting House), London's stone after Wren's St Paul's. Still quarried and mined.

regions.text: Isle of Portland, Dorset; used throughout the British Isles, above all in London's public buildings

materials.technology: Shipped by sea to London; Wren's choice for St Paul's made it London's stone; the railway reached the island in 1865.

examples.name: Banqueting House, Whitehall
examples.note: Inigo Jones, early 17th century

sources.title: Portland stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 98123)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Quarried since Roman times, it is one of Britain's best building stones, hence its use throughout the country.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is a limestone geological formation (formally named the Portland Stone Formation) dating to the Tithonian age of the Late Jurassic that is quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset, England

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It has been used extensively as a building stone throughout the British Isles, notably in major public buildings in London such as St Paul's Cathedral and Buckingham Palace.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Stone has been quarried on Portland since Roman times and was being shipped to London in the 14th century.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Extraction as an industry began in the early 17th century, with shipments to London for Inigo Jones' Banqueting House.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Wren's choice of Portland for the new St Paul's Cathedral was a great boost for the quarries and established Portland as London's choice of building stone.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The island was connected by railway to the rest of the country from 1865.

sources.title: Portland stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Albion Stone PLC has been quarrying and mining Portland stone since 1984.

materials.name: Purbeck Marble

period.text: Quarried since at least Roman times (43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for 'Roman'), when it was used for inscriptions, mouldings and veneers; one Bronze Age use, a cist at Langton Matravers, is not building. Used in the shafts, panels and floors of almost every medieval cathedral in the south of England; last extracted in 1993.

regions.text: Isle of Purbeck, Dorset (Worbarrow Tout to Peveril Point); used in cathedrals across the south of England and at Llandaff

materials.note: Not a true marble but a shelly limestone that takes a polish. Wikipedia dates the beds to the Early Cretaceous (Berriasian); FISH files Purbeck stone under Portland stone (Jurassic oolitic limestone).

sources.title: Purbeck stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 98131)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Collective name for the oolitic limestone quarried in the Isle of Purbeck region, geologically classified into two main groups.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It is a variety of Purbeck stone that has been quarried since at least Roman times as a decorative building stone.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Purbeck Marble is not a metamorphic rock, like a true marble, but is so-called because it can take a fine polish.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They were deposited during the Berriasian age of the Early Cretaceous epoch.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Purbeck Marble is found at outcrop, or beneath superficial cover, all the way across the Isle of Purbeck from Worbarrow Tout in the west to Peveril Point in the east.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There is a single example of Purbeck Marble being used during the Bronze Age, in a cist at Langton Matravers.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the Romano-British period, Purbeck Marble was used for inscriptions, architectural mouldings and veneers

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Purbeck Marble was also quarried in medieval times and can be seen in virtually all the cathedrals of the south of England, in columns and slab panels and flooring.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: For example, it is used in Exeter, Ely, Norwich, Chichester, Salisbury, Lincoln, Llandaff, Southwark and Canterbury Cathedrals, and in Westminster Abbey.

sources.title: Purbeck Marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Purbeck Marble was previously extracted in 1993.

materials.name: Kentish ragstone

period.text: Used in roughly squared blocks since Roman times (43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for 'Roman'; a Roman ship found at Blackfriars carried it); built Norman castles and churches from 1066, went out of fashion for brick in Tudor times, came back for Victorian Gothic churches. Still quarried for building at Hermitage Quarry.

regions.text: Quarried around Maidstone and along the Greensand Ridge in Kent; used in London and across South East England

materials.technology: Carried by boat down the Medway to London; the only hard building stone of the South East.

examples.name: Westminster Abbey
examples.note: rebuilding of the 1240s needed so much ragstone that a royal order reserved it

sources.title: Kentish ragstone (FISH Building Materials, concept 98003)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Sandy, rough blue to green/grey coloured limestone. Quarried in Kent and widely used throughout the South East.

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: a layer of limestones running from Kent into Surrey which was laid down in the Cretaceous period

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Since Roman times, ragstone has been used in roughly squared blocks for building walls.

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The stone was almost certainly quarried at the Tovil quarry near Maidstone, and then transported by boat along the River Medway to London.

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: With hard rock for building being in short supply in south-east England, it was inevitable that the only significant source of hard limestone – Kentish ragstone – would be used in building from an early period.

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From 1066, the Normans constructed a large number of public buildings using ragstone, such as Westminster Abbey and the Tower of London, castles such as Rochester and Leeds

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The building of Westminster Abbey in the 1240s required large quantities of ragstone with the result that local supplies were commandeered for that purpose

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: although in Tudor times stone buildings went out of fashion in favour of brick, the demand for Gothic-style buildings in Victorian times led to many churches in south-east East England being built of ragstone

sources.title: Kentish ragstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hermitage Quarry continues to meet the traditional demand for building stone for use in modern buildings.

period.text: Chosen by masons for 'more than 1000 years' says one source, so about 1000 at the latest, an approximate year and not a dated building; quarrying grew greatly in later Victorian times. Still quarried at two places on Ham Hill.

regions.text: Ham Hill, south Somerset; the medieval church towers of the county and the town of South Petherton

examples.name: Church of St Mary, Chedzoy
examples.note: doorway arches and bell openings of the tower

sources.title: Ham Hill stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 97963)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Shelly, gold/brown, coloured liassic limestone containing large quantities of crystalline calcite.

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In origin, Hamstone is a Jurassic limestone from the Toarcian, or Upper Lias, stage.

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The attractive colour also contributes to its being chosen by masons and architects for more than 1000 years for adorning the buildings in the countryside of surrounding Somerset.

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hamstone is featured in the medieval church towers throughout the county, and the town of South Petherton is built largely of the material.

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: hamstone is soft enough to be cut to make decorative features such as doorway arches and bell openings in church towers such as at the Church of St Mary at Chedzoy, Somerset

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In later Victorian times industrial quarrying expanded significantly

sources.title: Hamstone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Today hamstone is quarried in only two areas of Ham Hill.

period.text: The wool trade's best era, 1250-1350, paid for the Cotswold-stone 'wool churches': 1250 is the start of that era, not a dated building. The Cotswold style of stone houses emerged in the late 16th century and flourished through the 17th; the stone is still quarried.

regions.text: The Cotswolds: mainly Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire, and parts of Wiltshire, Somerset, Worcestershire and Warwickshire

sources.title: Cotswold stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 97863)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Sandy, light brown (cream to golden) coloured limestone, easily worked and readily available.

sources.title: Cotswolds
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The area is defined by the bedrock of Jurassic limestone that creates a type of grassland habitat that is quarried for the golden-coloured Cotswold stone.

sources.title: Cotswolds
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It lies across the boundaries of several English counties: mainly Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire, and parts of Wiltshire, Somerset, Worcestershire, and Warwickshire.

sources.title: Cotswolds
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The most successful era for the wool trade was 1250–1350

sources.title: Cotswolds
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The area still preserves numerous large, handsome Cotswold Stone "wool churches".

sources.title: Cotswold architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Cotswold style emerged during the late 16th century and flourished throughout the 17th century.

materials.name: Barnack stone

period.text: First used by the Romans (43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for 'Roman'); the medieval Fenland abbeys fought over it. The best stone was worked out by about 1460; lesser stone was quarried into the 18th century and, last, as roadstone in 1825.

regions.text: Barnack, near Stamford (now Peterborough); carried by water across the Fens to Peterborough, Ely, Crowland, Ramsey and Bury St Edmunds, and reused in Cambridge colleges

materials.technology: Blocks went by sledge to the Welland and by barge down the Nene and the Fenland waterways; after the Dissolution, stone from demolished monasteries was reused.

examples.name: St John the Baptist's Church, Barnack

sources.title: Lincolnshire limestone (FISH Building Materials, concept 98029; Barnack Stone a non-preferred term)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Generic term for the oolitic limestones quarried in Northamptonshire, Lincolnshire and Rutland.

sources.title: Lincolnshire Limestone Formation
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: part of the Inferior Oolite Group of the (Bajocian) Middle Jurassic strata of eastern England

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Oolitic Lincolnshire limestone, including some called Barnack rag, was a valuable building stone first used by the Romans.

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Quarrying continued in the Middle Ages when the abbeys at Peterborough, Crowland, Ramsey, Sawtry and Bury St Edmunds all used Barnack stone

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Blocks of stone were transported on sleds to the river Welland and loaded onto barges on which they were taken down the River Nene and the Fenland waterways.

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most notably, Barnack stone was used to build Peterborough and Ely Cathedrals.

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The stone was used for numerous buildings in Barnack itself, most notably the parish church.

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The best Barnack stone had been worked out by about 1460, but after the dissolution of the monasteries supplies became available from demolition of the Fenland monasteries and was reused in Cambridge colleges.

sources.title: Barnack
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lesser-quality Barnack stone continued to be quarried until the 18th century, and in 1825 it was quarried as roadstone for the Great North Road.

materials.name: Caen stone (imported from Normandy)

period.text: Not a stone of the isles: imported from Normandy. The Normans brought Romanesque building after the Conquest of 1066 and built the Tower of London and the cathedrals of Canterbury and Norwich partly of Caen stone; still used in the 19th century (Big Ben's clock tower). The trade ceased in the 1960s; quarrying in Normandy restarted in the 1980s, mainly for local work.

regions.text: Quarried near Caen, Normandy (France); used mainly in south-east and eastern England, carried by sea and river

materials.technology: Fine, even limestone easy to carve, shipped across the Channel and up rivers (to Norwich up the Wensum).
materials.note: Wikipedia gives the Caen limestone a Jurassic (Bathonian) age; FISH files Caen stone under Cretaceous limestone.

sources.title: Caen stone (FISH Building Materials, concept 97788)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Fine grained limestone, yellow or yellow/white in colour. Imported from France, mainly for ecclesiastical use.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: is a light creamy-yellow Jurassic limestone quarried in north-western France near the city of Caen

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The stone is homogeneous, and therefore suitable for carving.

sources.title: Norman architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Romanesque architecture was introduced to England after the Norman Conquest of 1066.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, Canterbury Cathedral, Westminster Abbey and the Tower of London were all partially built from imported Caen stone.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Used by the Normans for the cathedral and castle in Norwich, where it was brought by boat up the River Wensum.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Caen stone continued to be a popular material in Britain after the Norman period.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Underground mining developed in the 19th century, but the stone trade declined in the 20th century, eventually ceasing in the 1960s.

sources.title: Caen stone
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Excavation restarted in the 1980s with the stone being used for building the Caen Memorial.

materials.name: Aberdeen granite

period.text: Rubislaw Quarry opened in 1740 (another source says granite was quarried there for more than 300 years); Aberdeen was built of local grey granite from the mid-18th to the mid-20th century; Rubislaw closed in 1971.

regions.text: Aberdeen (the 'Granite City'); also sent to London for Waterloo Bridge and the terrace of the Palace of Westminster

materials.technology: Steam-powered cutting and polishing tools, invented by Alexander MacDonald of Aberdeen, made polished granite a Victorian status material from the 1830s.

examples.name: Marischal College
examples.note: Mackenzie's extension of 1906, the second-largest granite building in the world

materials.name: Red sandstones (Old and New Red Sandstone)

period.text: The stone keep of Goodrich Castle, Herefordshire, from the middle of the 12th century (1150 stands for 'about'), is the earliest dated building of Old Red Sandstone country a source names; Arbroath Abbey (founded 1178) is of local red sandstone. The Permian red sandstone of Locharbriggs, Dumfriesshire, has been worked since the 18th century and is still quarried.

regions.text: Old Red Sandstone: Stirling, Stonehaven, Perth and Tayside, Caithness; Herefordshire, Monmouthshire and Brecknockshire. New Red Sandstone: Locharbriggs near Dumfries, used in Dumfries, Glasgow and Edinburgh

materials.note: Not all 'red' sandstone is red: the Old Red Sandstone also runs to grey, green and purple, and Goodrich's keep is of light grey sandstone.

materials.name: Gritstone (Millstone Grit)

period.text: The Martello towers of 1804-1812, for which a source says Bramley Fall gritstone was ideal, are the earliest dated works the sources tie to it; the stone was used long before for millstones and walls, undated here. Bramley's quarries closed around 1930; Bramley Fall stone is still quarried near Leeds.

regions.text: The Pennines and neighbouring Northern England (the Dark Peak, Derbyshire, Yorkshire around Leeds), north-east Wales and north-west Ireland

materials.technology: Quarried for millstones (hence the name), building stone, paving flags and roofing; strong and resistant to water, so used for docks, locks, railways and engine beds.

sources.title: Gritstone (sandstone) (FISH Building Materials, concept 97957)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Carboniferous sandstone varying in grain size from coarse to fine and in colour from white, yellow, pink to brown.

sources.title: Millstone Grit
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Millstone Grit is any of a number of coarse-grained sandstones of Carboniferous age which occur in the British Isles.

sources.title: Millstone Grit
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The term gritstone describes any sandstone composed of coarse angular grains, and specifically refers to such sandstones within the Pennines and neighbouring areas of Northern England.

sources.title: Millstone Grit
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They also occur in parts of northeast Wales and northwest Ireland.

sources.title: Millstone Grit
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Various of the sandstone beds of the Millstone Grit have been quarried for building stone, paving flags and roofing material.

sources.title: Millstone Grit
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The very name of the rock derives from its widespread use within cornmills where it proved suitable for grinding stones.

sources.title: Bramley Fall stone

sources.title: Bramley Fall stone

materials.name: Kilkenny marble (Irish Carboniferous limestone)

period.text: The Black Quarry south of Kilkenny was worked from the 17th to the 19th century (1600 and 1899 stand for those centuries); stone of the same formation is still marketed as Kilkenny black marble.

regions.text: County Kilkenny (Archersgrove and Gallowshill; the 'Marble City') and County Carlow; used across Ireland

materials.technology: Water-driven saws at a weir on the Nore cut the blocks, with sand as the abrasive; offcuts were burnt for lime.

sources.title: Kilkenny marble

sources.title: Kilkenny marble

sources.quote: Produce from other quarries of Butlersgrove Formation stone continue to be marketed as "Kilkenny black marble" when polished, including Bannagagole Quarry near Oldleighlin, County Carlow.

sources.title: Kilkenny marble
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A weir on the river provided water to drive reciprocating cross-cut saws to cut the larger blocks into the finished shapes required for the market.

sources.title: Kilkenny marble
sources.author: Wikipedia

sources.title: Kilkenny marble

materials.name: Lime mortar

period.text: The Romans used lime mortars throughout their empire; 43, the year of the Roman conquest, stands for their arrival, and the Late Roman fort at Burgh Castle (third century) is the earliest building in the isles a source names as laid in lime mortar. Portland cement displaced it in new building through the 19th century; it is still used, above all in conservation.

materials.technology: Lime burnt in kilns, mostly at small coastal ports where limestone and coal came by sea; the railways made the small kilns unprofitable through the 19th century, and quick-setting, strong Portland cement replaced lime mortar in new work.

sources.title: Mortar (FISH Building Materials, concept 98062; Lime Mortar a non-preferred term)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A mixture of lime or more recently cement with sand and water used for bonding stones or bricks.

sources.title: Lime mortar
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Roman Empire used lime-based mortars extensively.

sources.title: Roman Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The occupation lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD.

sources.title: Flint
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Flint, knapped or unknapped, has been used from antiquity (for example at the Late Roman fort of Burgh Castle in Norfolk) up to the present day as a material for building stone walls, using lime mortar

sources.title: Lime mortar
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: With the introduction of Portland cement during the 19th century, the use of lime mortar in new constructions gradually declined. This was largely due to the ease of use of Portland cement, its quick setting, and high compressive strength.

sources.title: Lime mortar
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Lime mortar today is primarily used in the conservation of buildings originally built using it, but may be used as an alternative to ordinary portland cement.

sources.title: Lime kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Lime use in agriculture and coal"
sources.quote: Because land transportation of minerals like limestone and coal was difficult in the pre-industrial era, they were distributed by sea, and lime was most often manufactured at small coastal ports.

sources.title: Lime kiln
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The development of the national rail network made the local small-scale kilns increasingly unprofitable, and they gradually died out through the 19th century.

materials.name: Harling (lime render, Scotland and Ulster)

period.text: Scots building accounts use the word in 1540, when craftsmen harled the chapel, tennis court walls and turret at Falkland Palace: the earliest dated harling a source names. Still used on new buildings.

materials.technology: Lime render with pebbles or stone chips thrown on while wet, often limewashed; it sheds the wet climate. Cement harling, tried at the Hill House in 1904, trapped water and is not recommended.

materials.name: Roughcast and pebbledash

period.text: The Tudor period (from 1485), when glass fragments were sometimes set in it, is the earliest a source dates; the roughcast on St Albans' Norman tower was believed as old as the building but no year is given. Pebbledash spread in England and Wales in the 1920s; roughcast is still popular in Scotland and rural Ireland.

regions.text: Common houses and outbuildings throughout; pebbledash in England and Wales in the 1920s; still very popular in Scotland and rural Ireland

materials.technology: Lime, later cement, with sand and gravel thrown on with a trowel; in the 1920s builders used pebbledash to cover cheap brickwork.

examples.name: St Albans Cathedral
examples.note: roughcast on the central tower, removed around 1870

sources.title: Roughcast (FISH Building Materials, concept 98162)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A render including an aggregate of gravel or stone chipping thrown rather than trowelled onto an external wall.

sources.title: Roughcast
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They consist of lime and sometimes cement mixed with sand, small gravel and often pebbles or shells.

sources.title: Roughcast
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: in the Tudor period fragments of glass (frit) were sometimes embedded

sources.title: Roughcast
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: roughcast had been a widespread exterior coating given to the walls of common dwellings and outbuildings

sources.title: Roughcast
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This exterior wall finish was made popular in England and Wales during the 1920s, when housing was in greater demand, and house builders were forced to cut costs wherever they could, and used pebbledash to cover poor quality brick work

sources.title: Roughcast
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: However roughcasting remains very popular in Scotland and rural Ireland, with a high percentage of new houses being built with roughcasting.

sources.title: Roughcast

materials.name: Stucco

period.text: The Regency (strictly 1811-1820, its style applied before and after, to the end of William IV's reign in 1837) is the period a source ties to white painted stucco fronts; earlier Georgian use is not dated by these sources. Now made with cement and still used.

materials.technology: Lime and sand or brick dust at first, later cement (Portland cement is a basic ingredient of modern stucco); in the Cotswolds classical taste put stucco where limewash had been.

sources.title: Stucco (FISH Building Materials, concept 98220)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Smooth rendering applied to the exterior of buildings which may be incised to suggest coursed masonry. Made of lime and sand or brick dust, and more recently, cement.

sources.title: Regency architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many buildings of the Regency style have a white painted stucco façade

sources.title: Regency architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The British Regency strictly lasted only from 1811 to 1820, but the term is applied to architecture more widely, both before 1811 and after 1820

sources.title: Regency architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the next reign, of William IV from 1830 to 1837, has not been given its own stylistic descriptor

sources.title: Cotswold architecture
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Classical influences to the exteriors included the use of stucco on walls, which often replaced the limewash on original buildings.

sources.title: Portland cement
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Portland cement is the most common type of cement in general use around the world as a basic ingredient of concrete, mortar, stucco, and non-specialty grout.

links.claim: Rubble and ashlar are the two forms of stone walling and often share one wall: an ashlar face over a rubble core, as in medieval cathedrals.

sources.title: Ashlar

sources.quote: Ashlar masonry is in contrast to rubble masonry, which employs irregularly shaped stones

links.claim: Flushwork is a decorative form of knapped-flint walling, set flush with pale freestone, at its height in the 15th and early 16th centuries.

sources.title: Flushwork

links.claim: In higher-status buildings, galleted joints gave way to flints knapped square, which leave little mortar showing.

sources.title: Galleting
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In higher status buildings, galleting was superseded by square knapping the flints to produce flat, squared stones that produced a surface with little exposed mortar.

links.claim: Portland cement, introduced in the 19th century, gradually replaced lime mortar in new building because it was easier to use, set quickly and was stronger.

sources.quote: A mixture of lime or more recently cement with sand and water used for bonding stones or bricks.

sources.title: Portland cement
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was developed from other types of hydraulic lime in England in the early 19th century by Joseph Aspdin

links.claim: Joseph Aspdin named his patent cement of 1824 after Portland stone, which it resembled once hardened: an influence of name and look, not of material.

sources.title: Portland cement
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The cement was so named by Joseph Aspdin, who obtained a patent for it in 1824, because, once hardened, it resembled the fine, pale limestone known as Portland stone

sources.title: Portland cement (FISH Building Materials, concept 98121)
